headline: High: shared broad network and file access create leakage and conflict risks; LangGraph’s orchestration can cascade RD-Agent outputs into actions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LangGraph can read/write application files and run browsers, while RD-Agent also runs browsers and uses files/logs. That creates a plausible content-bridging path where attacker-controlled web or file content from one side can be treated as instructions by the other. The pair lacks documented provenance isolation, so uncertainty stays medium rather than low.
conditions: IF either agent ingests browser-rendered or file-based content as instructions without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF the two agents exchange artifacts through shared files or logs, attacker-controlled text can bridge them.
mitigations: Add a provenance tag to every exchanged artifact.
Disable automatic instruction-following from file or browser content.
Separate workspaces for the two agents.
Review any shared prompt templates for untrusted content handling.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents have broad network egress and touch sensitive operational data: LangGraph handles model-provider secrets and application state, while RD-Agent handles API keys plus financial reports, competition datasets, execution traces, and logs. If they share a workspace or checkpointer-backed state, either side can expose the other’s data to external APIs. The pairwise leakage path is credible and high impact.
conditions: IF the two agents share a filesystem, checkpointer store, or environment variables, sensitive data can cross-contaminate.
IF RD-Agent sends logs or traces containing LangGraph state to external APIs, leakage occurs.
mitigations: Use separate secrets stores for each agent.
Put each agent in a distinct workspace or container.
Redact logs before any API call.
Disable sharing of checkpointer state across agents.
Rotate exposed API keys immediately after any shared-run test.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: LangGraph can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses; RD-Agent also uses files and broad network egress, with multiple instances supported. Even without explicit git overlap, shared mutable resources can race through the checkpointer or log directories. The conflict is real in default orchestration setups, but not enough evidence for high because git writes are not documented for both.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or state store, last-writer-wins conflicts can corrupt outputs.
IF the orchestrator does not lock shared state, concurrent runs can overwrite each other.
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories.
Enable locking on shared state stores.
Run only one writer per workspace.
Add timestamped filenames for artifacts.
requires-engineering: implement optimistic concurrency checks.

D_cascading_error.rationale: LangGraph is an orchestration framework that can route outputs into downstream nodes, and RD-Agent is a research/automation agent that produces logs, traces, and API-driven outputs. If LangGraph treats RD-Agent outputs as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into further actions or reports. The interaction is plausible by design, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF LangGraph forwards RD-Agent outputs into downstream nodes without verification, errors cascade.
IF downstream nodes take actions based on RD-Agent-generated facts, the blast radius expands.
mitigations: Insert a verification step between agents.
Require citations for any factual claim before reuse.
Limit downstream actions to read-only mode.
Add human approval for irreversible steps.
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks.

E_compliance.rationale: RD-Agent explicitly touches financial reports, competition datasets, execution traces, and logs, while LangGraph handles application-defined graph state and model-provider secrets. The profiles do not document residency or retention controls, so a compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. Because both are open-source and the interaction is undocumented, uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into RD-Agent logs or LangGraph state, retention and residency obligations may be triggered.
IF either deployment stores data in a region or vendor path not approved for that data class, compliance gaps arise.
mitigations: Classify data before either agent sees it.
Disable logging of regulated fields.
Pin deployments to approved regions.
Review retention settings for both systems.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data residency and deletion.
